Load packages and datasets

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(brms)

dat_dich <- read.csv("data/rubin_2024_crita.csv")
dat_dich <- dat_dich |> rename(y = crit_a)
```

# Continuous example

## Fit continuous model

Use the ordinal dataset and show bad model fit visually. Mention problems with comparing continuous and ordinal likelihoods based on loo.

brms code baseline model:

```{r}
#| eval: false
f_cont <- bf(
  y ~ 1 + (1 | rater) + (1 | subject)
)

# Priors
priors_cont <- c(
  prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "sd", group = "rater"),
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "sd", group = "subject"),
  prior(exponential(1), class = "sigma")
)

# Fit
fit_cont <- brm(
  formula = f_cont,
  data = dat_cont,
  family = gaussian(link = "identity"),
  prior = priors_cont,

  chains = 4,
  cores = 4
)
```

## Demonstrate theoretical equivalence

Show for the standard continuous multilevel model that:

- ICCs can also be computed based on posterior predictive simulations instead of ratios of variance components
- ICC computation based on variance components match the intra-class correlations under specific rater scenarios.

*Auszug aus der Diagnostik 2 Vorlesung:*

>Jede ICC kann als Schätzwert
für die Korrelation zwischen zwei Ratings
der gleichen Personen in der Population
interpretiert werden:
>- ICC(1,1): Für jede Person werden die beiden Rater zufällig gezogen.
(In Modell 1 können die Rater ohnehin nicht identifiziert werden)
>- ICC(2,1): Für jede Person werden die beiden Rater zufällig gezogen.
Jede Person wird also von zwei neuen Ratern beurteilt.
>- ICC(3,1): Es werden zwei Rater (Rater 1 und Rater 2) zufällig gezogen und diese beiden Rater beurteilen alle Personen.
>
>Für die average ICCs bezieht sich die Korrelation analog auf zwei mittlere
Ratings (mittleres Rating 1 und 2) der gleichen Personen.


# Dichotomous example

## Prior predictive checks

Sample predictions from the priors

```{r}
f_dich <- bf(
  y ~ 1 + (1 | rater) + (1 | subject),
  family = bernoulli(link = "logit"),
  center = FALSE
)
priors_dich <- c(
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", coef = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "sd", group = "rater"),
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "sd", group = "subject")
)
fit_dich <- brm(
  formula = f_dich,
  prior = priors_dich,
  data = dat_dich,
  seed = 42,
  chains = 4,
  cores = 4,
  sample_prior = "only"
)
```

compute prior predictive checks

**TODO:** Think of a small set of informative and intuitive checks and plot them (e.g. 2 x 2 panel)

```{r}
#| message: false
# prior predictive checks

d <- na.omit(fit_dich$data[, c("y", "rater", "subject")])

# Overall prevalence
pp_check(fit_dich, newdata = d, type = "stat",
         stat = "mean", prefix = "ppd")

# probability that a pair of randomly drawn raters agrees
agreement <- function(y) {
  n <- table(dat_dich$subject, y)
  sum(choose(n, 2)) / sum(choose(rowSums(n), 2))
}

pp_check(fit_dich, type = "stat", stat = "agreement", prefix = "ppd")
```
